```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# ranger fits the random forest, sp the GWR, gstat the variograms behind the
# autocorrelation ranges, and ggplot2 draws the figures. All four are
# Suggests, so the article is gated on them and R CMD build succeeds without
# them.
# `eval` gates chunks only: knitr does not apply it to inline `r ...` code,
# which runs regardless. An inline reference to something a chunk defines
# has to guard itself, as in `r if (runs) x else NA`, or the article fails
# to build where a package is missing.
has_ranger <- requireNamespace("ranger",  quietly = TRUE)
has_sp     <- requireNamespace("sp",      quietly = TRUE)
has_gstat  <- requireNamespace("gstat",   quietly = TRUE)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
runs <- has_ranger && has_sp && has_gstat && has_ggplot

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo      = TRUE,
  message   = FALSE,
  warning   = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%",
  eval      = runs
)
```

```{r missing-deps, echo=FALSE, eval=!runs, results='asis'}
cat("*(The code below needs `ranger`, `sp`, `gstat` and `ggplot2`, and at",
    "least one of them is not installed here, so it is shown but not run.",
    "`install.packages(c(\"ranger\", \"sp\", \"gstat\", \"ggplot2\"))`",
    "installs them.)*\n")
```

A cross-validated score says how far the predictions fell from held-out
values. It does not say whether the model left spatial structure in its
residuals, or at which locations the score applies. This article fits the
random forest and GWR on one simulated field and shows the code for the
Bayesian GP, writes a backend of its own, scores them on the same folds, and
then answers those two questions. It also shows how to
choose predictors without letting the choice see the held-out rows.

*This article needs four optional packages: `ranger` for the random forest,
`sp` for GWR, `gstat` for the autocorrelation ranges and `ggplot2` for the
figures. Without them the code is shown but not run.*

## Choosing a backend

The package fits three backends behind one `spatial_fit` class, so the
functions that check, compare and map a fit take any of them. `compare_models_cv()` scores them
on the same folds. Before running it, pick the candidates by what each
backend gives you:

| Backend | Use it for | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| Random forest, `fit_rf_model()` | nonlinear effects and interactions you do not write down; permutation importance in place of coefficients | `ranger` |
| GWR, `fit_gwr_model()` | coefficients that vary across the map, which you can map and interpret | `sp` |
| Bayesian GP, `fit_bayesian_spatial_model()` | a posterior distribution: predictive intervals, a standard error for each point of a surface, and the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS); count, binary, ordinal and categorical responses through `family` | `brms` and a C++ toolchain |

The random forest is the cheapest to fit and to cross-validate. Each fold of
`cv_bayes()` is a full MCMC (Markov chain Monte Carlo) run, so the Bayesian GP is by far the slowest of
the three, with GWR between them.

No backend fixes folds that are wrong for the map. All three can predict from
location, the forest when it is given the coordinates, so the fold scheme has
to match the distances the map predicts at before a comparison of backends
means anything; `vignette("spatial-cross-validation")` covers that. If the
question is only whether the predictors miss spatial structure,
`residual_morans_i()` on the cheapest fit you can make answers it before you
pick a backend.

## A simulated field

One real predictor, `a`, and a spatial field that no predictor carries drive
the response; `b` is noise. The field has an exponential covariance with
range parameter 70 m, so its correlation falls to 5 percent at about 210 m,
three times the range parameter.

```{r fixture}
library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

set.seed(11)
n  <- 350
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
field <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 70) + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n))
xy$a  <- rnorm(n)
xy$b  <- rnorm(n)
xy$z  <- 1.5 * xy$a + field + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
pts   <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
```

## The three backends

### Random forest

```{r rf}
rf <- fit_rf_model(pts, "z", c("a", "b"))
rf
```

The forest's fitted values, and so its R² and residuals, are out-of-bag: each
row is predicted by the trees whose bootstrap sample left it out. The last
lines of the print say what that random hold-out measures.

### GWR, with a map of its coefficients

```{r gwr}
gwr <- fit_gwr_model(pts, "z", c("a", "b"))
gwr
```

Each location gets its own regression, weighted towards its nearest
neighbours, and `coef.gwr_fit()` returns one row of coefficients per
location. `plot.spatial_fit()` maps one of them:

```{r gwr-map, fig.height=4.5, fig.alt=if (runs) sprintf("Map of the local intercept of the GWR fit at the %d training points, from %.1f to %.1f, in patches that follow the simulated field.", nrow(pts), min(coef(gwr)[, 'Intercept']), max(coef(gwr)[, 'Intercept'])) else "Map of the local intercept of the GWR fit at the training points."}
plot(gwr, type = "coefficients", term = "Intercept")
```

```{r gwr-numbers, include=FALSE}
b_gwr   <- coef(gwr)
r_field <- cor(b_gwr[, "Intercept"], field)
a_range <- range(b_gwr[, "a"])
```

The local intercept takes up the field the predictors miss: its correlation
with the simulated field is `r if (runs) sprintf("%.2f", r_field) else NA`.
The local coefficient of `a` runs from
`r if (runs) sprintf("%.2f", a_range[1]) else NA` to
`r if (runs) sprintf("%.2f", a_range[2]) else NA`, around a true value of 1.5
that is the same everywhere. A map of a local coefficient shows estimation
noise as well as real variation.

### Bayesian GP

The Bayesian GP models the residual spatial structure as a Gaussian process
over the coordinates. The chunk below is shown but not run. The fit needs
`brms` and a C++ toolchain, and compiling and sampling it takes longer than
the rest of this article together.

```{r bayes, eval=FALSE}
bayes <- fit_bayesian_spatial_model(pts, "z", c("a", "b"),
                                    chains = 2, iter = 1000, seed = 1)
bayes
```

On this field the fit warns that the autocorrelation range sits below what
its default basis resolves, and names the `gp_resolution` that would resolve
it. "What the basis resolves" on `?fit_bayesian_spatial_model` explains the
floor. `predictor_vars = character(0)` fits a GP with an intercept alone,
which shows how much of the surface the spatial term carries without the
predictors.

## Writing your own backend

Any model can join the comparison once it is wrapped as a `spatial_fit`, the
object the checks in this article take. The function below fits a
linear model and passes it to `new_spatial_fit()` with the formula, the
response, the predictors and the training rows. `subclass` names the class
the methods dispatch on. `cv_spatial()` scores each fold through `predict()`,
and `summary.spatial_fit()` and `model_metrics()` need `fitted()`, so the
backend defines both; `residuals()` is optional.

```{r learner}
lm_fit <- function(train_sf, response_var = "z", predictor_vars = c("a", "b")) {
  d   <- st_drop_geometry(train_sf)
  # With no predictors the model is intercept-only: "z ~ 1", not "z ~ ".
  rhs <- if (length(predictor_vars)) paste(predictor_vars, collapse = " + ") else "1"
  fml <- as.formula(paste(response_var, "~", rhs))
  new_spatial_fit(
    subclass       = "lm_fit",
    engine         = lm(fml, data = d),
    formula        = fml,
    response_var   = response_var,
    predictor_vars = predictor_vars,
    data_sf        = train_sf
  )
}
predict.lm_fit <- function(object, newdata = NULL, ...) {
  if (is.null(newdata)) return(fitted(object$engine))
  as.numeric(predict(object$engine, newdata = st_drop_geometry(newdata)))
}
residuals.lm_fit <- function(object, ...) residuals(object$engine)
fitted.lm_fit    <- function(object, ...) fitted(object$engine)
# Registered so that spatialkit's own calls find the methods wherever this
# code runs; at the top level of a script they are found without it.
for (g in c("predict", "residuals", "fitted"))
  registerS3method(g, "lm_fit", get(paste0(g, ".lm_fit")))

fit <- lm_fit(pts)
fit
```

The linear model sees `a` and `b` and nothing of the field, so the field
stays in its residuals, a known error for the checks below to find.
`?new_spatial_fit` gives the
full contract, including the `coef()` method a backend with coefficients
should define.

## Comparing backends on the same folds

The folds hold out whole blocks of the map. `block_size` is the smallest
block edge to build, in metres here:

```{r folds}
folds <- make_folds(pts, k = 4, method = "block_kfold", block_size = 400,
                    seed = 1)
round(c(width  = folds$params$block_width,
        height = folds$params$block_height))
```

The square splits into `r if (runs) folds$params$n_blocks else NA` blocks,
one per fold, each wider than the 400 m asked for.

`compare_models_cv()` scores the built-in backends on those folds, and
`cv_spatial()` scores the linear model on the same ones, so the rows of the
table below are comparable:

```{r compare, warning=TRUE}
cmp   <- compare_models_cv(pts, "z", c("a", "b"), models = c("RF", "GWR"),
                           folds = folds, quiet = TRUE)
cv_lm <- cv_spatial(pts, "z", c("a", "b"), fit_fn = lm_fit, folds = folds)

scores <- rbind(cmp$overall, cbind(cv_lm$overall, model = "lm"))
scores[, c("model", "RMSE", "MAE", "R2", "n_pred")]
```

```{r compare-numbers, include=FALSE}
rmse <- setNames(scores$RMSE, scores$model)
```

GWR has the lowest RMSE (`r if (runs) sprintf("%.3f", rmse[["GWR"]]) else NA`
against `r if (runs) sprintf("%.3f", rmse[["lm"]]) else NA` for the linear
model and `r if (runs) sprintf("%.3f", rmse[["RF"]]) else NA` for the
forest), because its local intercept carries the field across the edges of
the held-out blocks, where held-out points sit close to training points. The forest has no coordinates here and does worst. The warning comes
from `cv_gwr()`: with a whole block held out, a few held-out points lie
farther from every training point than any of the fold's local regressions
reach, so their predictions are extrapolations in space. Blocked folds hold
out whole blocks to score predictions at that distance, so these points stay
in the score; keep such points out of a map unless you mean to extrapolate.

`cmp$by_fold` has the per-fold scores, and `plot_cv_metrics()` draws them.
To add the Bayesian GP, put `"Bayesian"` in `models` and its sampler settings
in `bayes_args`. The call is shown but not run, for the reason given above;
`overall` then also carries the held-out coverage of the GP's intervals and
its CRPS.

```{r compare-bayes, eval=FALSE}
cmp_all <- compare_models_cv(pts, "z", c("a", "b"),
                             models = c("RF", "GWR", "Bayesian"),
                             folds = folds,
                             bayes_args = list(chains = 2, iter = 1000))
cmp_all$overall
```

## Checking the residuals for spatial structure

```{r moran}
mi <- residual_morans_i(fit)
mi
```

A large positive Moran's I says nearby residuals resemble each other, so the
model is missing something that varies smoothly across the map. Here that is
the simulated field, by construction. The weights are each point's 8 nearest
neighbours, row-standardised; `k` changes the count and `weights` takes a
matrix of your own.

The `null` line says which moments the p-value came from. `residual` moments
condition on the design matrix and are exact for least-squares residuals;
`randomisation` moments treat the residuals as exchangeable and are an
approximation for any model. `null = "auto"` chooses per fit, so read what it
chose. The design rank is the rank of the rebuilt model matrix, which gives
the residual degrees of freedom. The kurtosis says how far the residuals sit
from the Gaussian case the moments assume, with 3 as the reference.

`plot.spatial_fit()` maps the residuals and shows where the structure is:

```{r resid-map, fig.height=4.5, fig.alt="Map of the linear model's residuals at the training points. Positive and negative residuals sit in patches rather than mixed at random, the structure Moran's I measures."}
plot(fit, type = "residuals")
```

The weight matrix is n by n, so the result describes it instead of returning
it. Ask for it when you want to reuse the same neighbours:

```{r keep-weights}
mi_w <- residual_morans_i(fit, keep_weights = TRUE)
dim(mi_w$weights)
str(mi$weights_summary[c("n", "storage", "neighbours", "kept")])
```

`weights_summary` is there either way, so a `NULL` in `weights` always comes
with its reason.

When the statistic is large, add a predictor that carries the missing
structure, if you have one, or fit a backend that models it, and test the
new fit's residuals:

```{r moran-gwr}
mi_gwr <- residual_morans_i(gwr)
round(c(lm = mi$observed, gwr = mi_gwr$observed), 3)
```

GWR's residuals are in-sample, so a lower I shows that the fit absorbed the
structure. The scores on held-out blocks in the previous section show
whether it also predicts better away from the data.

## Coordinates as predictors

A model given `x` and `y` can reproduce the training surface by memorising
location, so its error grows quickly with the distance from the data.
Random folds score it at the spacing of the samples, where memorised
locations help most. `fit_rf_model()` with `include_coords = TRUE` logs a
caution, once per session, for this reason. Score any such model on folds at
the distances its map will predict at; `vignette("spatial-cross-validation")`
shows how to match the two.

## Choosing predictors inside the folds

Choosing predictors on all the data and then cross-validating the chosen set
gives the selection a look at every held-out row. `select_features_forward()`
does the selection inside its own cross-validation, and takes a fold scheme
for it, because the variables chosen depend on how far the held-out rows sit
from the training rows. Blocked folds keep held-out rows apart from training
rows only if the blocks are at least as wide as the autocorrelation range,
and `make_folds()` warns when they are narrower. The range that counts is
that of what the candidates leave unexplained, the residuals of `z` on `a`
and `b`, which hold the field and the noise:

```{r sac}
sac <- estimate_sac_range(pts, "z", predictor_vars = c("a", "b"))
sac
```

At about `r if (runs) round(as.numeric(sac)) else NA` m, longer than the
field's 210 m, it is still below the 400 m minimum block edge passed to the
selection:

```{r selection}
# select_features_forward() calls fit_fn(train_sf, vars), so the learner above
# needs an adapter that puts `vars` in the predictor slot. Step 0 fits it with
# no predictors at all, which is why lm_fit() builds "z ~ 1" for an empty set.
sel_fn <- function(train_sf, vars) lm_fit(train_sf, "z", vars)

sel <- select_features_forward(pts, "z", c("a", "b"), fit_fn = sel_fn,
                               k = 4, method = "block_kfold",
                               block_size = 400, seed = 1)
sel$selected
sel$history
```

`history` has one row per candidate scored at each step. Step 0 is the
intercept-only model, so `a` had to beat it to be added, and at step 2 adding
the noise variable `b` made the cross-validated RMSE slightly worse, so the
selection stopped at `a`. A candidate is added when its pooled `gain` exceeds
`tol` and the mean of its per-fold gains (`fold_gain`) exceeds one standard
error of that mean (`fold_gain_se`); `rule = "tol"` tests the pooled gain
alone.

The selection's inner folds are `block_kfold` unless `method` names another
scheme, whatever folds the outer loop uses. Passing `random_kfold` there logs
a caution: random inner folds choose the variables that predict best at the
spacing of the samples, where one that only tracks nearby values of the
response can win. A blocked outer loop then scores the chosen set at the
blocks' distance, for which it was not chosen.

The call above is the inner step. Its own score has seen every row, so it is
not an estimate of the error of the chosen model. For that, run the selection
inside the `fit_fn` you pass to `cv_spatial()`: each outer fold then chooses
on its training rows alone and is scored on rows the choice never saw. With
`auto_range = TRUE` each training set's own autocorrelation range sizes its
inner blocks.

```{r nested}
chosen <- list()    # the set each outer fold chooses, kept to print below
select_then_fit <- function(train_sf) {
  s <- select_features_forward(train_sf, "z", c("a", "b"), fit_fn = sel_fn,
                               k = 3, auto_range = TRUE, seed = 1,
                               quiet = TRUE)
  chosen[[length(chosen) + 1]] <<- s$selected
  lm_fit(train_sf, "z", s$selected)
}
nested <- cv_spatial(pts, "z", c("a", "b"), fit_fn = select_then_fit,
                     folds = folds)
nested$overall[, c("RMSE", "MAE", "R2", "n_pred")]
vapply(chosen, paste, character(1), collapse = " + ")
```

The outer folds are the ones the backends were compared on, so the RMSE of
the selected model, `r if (runs) sprintf("%.3f", nested$overall$RMSE) else NA`,
sits beside the linear model's `r if (runs) sprintf("%.3f", rmse[["lm"]]) else NA`
on both predictors. Every outer fold chose `a`, so the nested score is that
of the linear model on `a` alone. The selection call in the previous chunk
reports the same score for `a` at step 1 because it built these same four
folds. The selection costs a full sweep per outer fold;
`?select_features_forward` gives the count of fits.

## Predicting a surface, and where the score applies

A cross-validated score describes predictions at predictor values like those
in the training data. `area_of_applicability()` measures how far each
prediction location's predictors sit from the training data's (the
dissimilarity index of Meyer and Pebesma 2021) and marks the locations beyond
a threshold. For a model whose predictions depend on location, such as a GWR
fit, it measures the distance to the training points as well.

The prediction locations below are the centres of a square grid over the
training area, with predictor values drawn for them. `b` is drawn three
standard deviations above its training mean, and one value of `a` is
missing.

```{r surface}
hull <- clip_target_for(pts, expand = 0.02, quiet = TRUE)
grid <- create_grid_polygons(hull, target_cells = 200, type = "square")
gp   <- suppressWarnings(st_centroid(grid))
set.seed(2)
gp$a <- rnorm(nrow(gp))
gp$b <- rnorm(nrow(gp), mean = 3)     # centred three standard deviations above the training mean
gp$a[1] <- NA                         # one missing predictor value

surface <- predict_surface(gwr, grid = gp)
```

Pass the folds the model was scored on. The threshold is then set by the
dissimilarity at which the cross-validated score was earned:

```{r aoa}
aoa <- area_of_applicability(gp, model = gwr, folds = folds)
aoa
```

```{r aoa-plot, fig.height=4.5, fig.alt=if (runs) sprintf("Cumulative distribution of the dissimilarity index. The training points, each measured to the nearest point outside its fold, rise steeply below the dashed threshold; the prediction locations rise more slowly, and %d of the %d with all predictors lie beyond it.", aoa$n_outside, aoa$n_new - aoa$n_na) else "Cumulative distribution of the dissimilarity index for the training points and the prediction locations, with the threshold dashed."}
plot(aoa)
```

The dissimilarity index `DI` is on `aoa$aoa`, beside the logical `AOA`, and
`threshold` is the cut-off derived from the training data. With `b` shifted,
`r if (runs) aoa$n_outside else NA` of the
`r if (runs) aoa$n_new - aoa$n_na else NA` locations with all predictors lie
outside the area the score covers.

`AOA` is `NA` where a predictor is missing or not finite, and `!NA` is `NA`.
So `sum(aoa$aoa$AOA)` returns `NA`, `surface[!aoa$aoa$AOA, ]` returns a row
of `NA`, and an assignment such as `x[!aoa$aoa$AOA] <- NA` skips that row.
Test for `TRUE`:

```{r aoa-na}
inside <- aoa$aoa$AOA %in% TRUE
c(inside = sum(inside), outside = aoa$n_outside, unknown = aoa$n_na)
```

Outside the area of applicability, mask the predictions, report the share
that was masked, and treat any prediction you keep there as an
extrapolation the score does not cover. To bring more of the map inside,
collect observations where the predictors take values the training data
lack.

```{r aoa-mask}
surface$.pred[!inside] <- NA
round(100 * mean(!inside), 1)    # percent of locations masked
```

## Next

The next article in reading order is `vignette("reporting")`, which says
which of these numbers to report and how. This article relied on
`?fit_rf_model`, `?fit_gwr_model`, `?fit_bayesian_spatial_model`,
`?new_spatial_fit`, `?compare_models_cv`, `?cv_spatial`,
`?residual_morans_i`, `?select_features_forward`, `?predict_surface` and
`?area_of_applicability`. `vignette("spatial-cross-validation")` covers fold
schemes and block sizes, and `vignette("glossary")` defines the terms used
here.

## References

Meyer, H. and Pebesma, E. (2021). Predicting into unknown space? Estimating
the area of applicability of spatial prediction models. *Methods in Ecology
and Evolution* 12(9), 1620–1633.
<https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13650>
